aiOverview.content: The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) is the EU's authority for aviation safety, ensuring high standards, environmental protection, and certification across EU Member States. Based in Cologne, it regulates airworthiness, pilot licensing, and aerodromes. EASA promotes safer, greener, and more connected air travel. Key Aspects of EASA Role & Function: EASA harmonizes regulations, type certifies aircraft components, approves design/manufacturing organizations, and manages the "EU air safety list" of banned operators. Safety & Security: It provides safety oversight and technical expertise, including updating Conflict Zone Information Bulletins (CZIB) for risk assessment. Sustainability: EASA works to improve the environmental impact of aviation, such as evaluating CO2cap C cap O sub 2𝐶𝑂2 emissions. Eligibility & Structure: It is an agency of the European Commission with a Management Board representing EU Member States. It operates with a budget partly funded by the EU and partly through industry certification fees. Location: Cologne, Germany (headquarters) with a satellite office in Brussels. Note: There is another entity known as "EASA" (The Electro•Mechanical Authority), which is a separate organization for the electrical repair industry.
